sections.summary: The greeting identifies the audience as those who 'received a faith of the same kind as ours' by divine allotment (lachousin, from lanchano) and by the righteousness of God, with grace and peace multiplied through the knowledge (epignosis) of God and Jesus.
sections.relevance: The verb lanchano ('to obtain by lot, to receive by allotment, to be granted') explicitly presents faith as something the audience received from God rather than something they generated by their own effort. The neutral reading states: 'The audience did not produce their faith by their own effort; they received it. The verb carries the connotation of divine allotment.' This language leans toward God as the source and distributor of faith, which has implications for who determines salvation. However, the primary concern of the passage is not individual predetermination but the equal standing (isotimos) of Gentile and apostolic faith -- a corporate inclusion point paralleling Acts 15:9. The passage does not address whether human response plays a role in receiving this allotted faith, and the allotment language may describe God's extension of covenant faith to Gentiles as a group rather than his selection of specific individuals.
key_phrases: received a faith of the same kind as ours
by the righteousness of our God and Savior
grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God

sections.section_title: What the Divine Power Has Provided
sections.summary: God's divine power has granted everything pertaining to life and godliness through the knowledge of Christ, and through his precious promises the audience may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world by desire.
sections.relevance: This section emphasizes God's comprehensive initiative: divine power granted everything needed, God called the audience, God provided promises. However, the neutral reading explicitly frames these indicatives as the foundation for the imperatives that follow: 'Every imperative that follows in verses 5-11 rests on the indicatives stated here.' The structure is provision-then-response, which implies that divine provision enables but does not replace human agency. The purpose clause 'so that through these you may become (genesthe, subjunctive) partakers of the divine nature' indicates potential and purpose rather than certainty -- God provides so that the audience may participate, not so that they inevitably will. Furthermore, the neutral reading notes that the accomplished escape from corruption (aorist participle apophygontes) can be undone, since the author himself will describe people who 'escaped the defilements of the world' but became 'again entangled' (2:20). The framework is one of enablement: God removes every obstacle and provides every resource, placing the responsibility for the outcome squarely on the human response.
key_phrases: His divine power has granted to us everything pertaining to life and godliness
through the knowledge of Him who called us
so that through these you may become partakers of the divine nature
having escaped the corruption that is in the world by desire

sections.summary: The audience is commanded to apply all diligence to supplement their faith with a chain of virtues: moral excellence, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly kindness, and love -- each building cumulatively on the one before.
sections.relevance: The neutral reading is explicit: 'The imperatives are not arbitrary demands but the required human response to the completed divine provision. God has given everything; the audience must now do something with what they have received.' The verb pareisphero ('to bring alongside, to contribute, to add one's own effort to what is already present') attributes genuine effort to the audience. The word spoude ('eagerness, diligence, earnestness') is described as 'a hallmark of the letter: the audience must exercise urgent, active effort. The provision is God's; the diligence is theirs.' The entire chain presupposes that the audience can and must actively cultivate these qualities -- the virtues are not automatically conferred by divine provision but must be generously supplied through human effort. This section directly presents human agency as necessary in the spiritual life, though the explicit connection to salvation outcomes appears in the following section.
key_phrases: in your faith supply moral excellence
add one's own effort to what is already present
The provision is God's; the diligence is theirs

sections.summary: The presence and growth of the virtues renders a person fruitful in the knowledge of Christ; their absence renders a person blind and forgetful of purification; the audience is commanded to make their calling and election firm through practice, with the conditional promise that they will never stumble and will receive a richly supplied entrance into the eternal kingdom.
sections.relevance: This section directly addresses salvation outcomes and makes them contingent on human conduct. The neutral reading states: 'The logic is conditional: the outcome depends on whether the qualities of verses 5-7 are present and growing.' The command to make calling and election 'firm' (bebaian) acknowledges that calling and election originate with God, but presents their confirmation as a human responsibility: 'God calls and elects; the human being confirms that calling and election by living in accordance with it. The calling is God's initiative; the confirmation is the human response that validates and solidifies it.' The conditional promise 'as long as you practice these things, you will never stumble' is explicitly noted: 'The promise is not that stumbling is impossible regardless of conduct but that stumbling will not occur as long as these qualities are actively practiced and growing.' The entrance into the eternal kingdom (v. 11) is the salvation outcome, and it is richly supplied to those who practice the virtues -- implicitly withheld from those who do not. The person who lacks the virtues is 'blind, short-sighted, having forgotten the purification from his former sins' (v. 9) -- a portrait the neutral reading identifies as the precursor to the full description of false teachers in chapter 2 who escaped corruption but returned to it. The entire section presents human choices as determining whether God's provision achieves its intended purpose in a given person's life.
key_phrases: if these qualities are yours and are increasing
the one who lacks these qualities is blind or short-sighted, having forgotten the purification from his former sins
be all the more diligent to make certain about His calling and choosing you
as long as you practice these things, you will never stumble
the entrance into the eternal kingdom will be richly supplied to you

sections.section_title: The Reason for Writing -- Peter's Impending Death
sections.summary: Peter explains that his death is imminent (as Christ disclosed to him) and that he writes to leave a permanent reminder of these teachings so the community can recall them after his departure.

sections.section_title: Eyewitness of Christ's Majesty at the Transfiguration
sections.summary: Peter grounds the apostolic proclamation of Christ's power and coming (parousia) in the eyewitness experience of the transfiguration, where he saw Christ receive honor and glory and heard the voice from the Majestic Glory identifying Jesus as God's beloved Son.

The prophetic word is confirmed by the transfiguration experience and functions as a lamp in a dark place until the day of Christ's return dawns; prophecy originated not from human will but from men moved by the Holy Spirit who spoke from God.
